prime.problem: Reading formulas is not the same as using them under pressure. Asked how many 128k users fit on this box? or how big a batch does this MoE need?, you have to pick the right formula, fill it and sanity-check it in minutes. Without practice, the chapter stays recognisable but not usable.
prime.fits: Fourteenth card: the seven problems at the end of Part 7, all on one invented model on a TPU v5e 4x4. They call on parameter counting and KV bytes, the step-time floor, sharding, MoE's B<sub>crit</sub> and 2D weight-stationary sharding.
expect: MoE: total vs active, B<sub>crit</sub> × E/k
prime.goal: Solve each problem type from a blank page, check the answer against a second estimate, and say which everyday question each one models.

attend: In Q1, which block holds 70% of the weights, and why doesn't the embedding matter much here?
In Q2, why does dropping to one KV head multiply the batch by 8 but leave the parameter count almost unchanged?
Q3 calls the weight-load time a lower bound on per-step latency. Why is it a floor, and what usually sits on top of it?
In Q5, why do total parameters scale with E but FLOPs only with k, and what does that do to B<sub>crit</sub>?
In Q7, why does 2D sharding's communication fall as √N while 1D's stays flat?

must: Count parameters by block (MLP 3·D·F, attention 2·D·H·(N+K), embeddings D·V) per layer → weight bytes → divide by total HBM bandwidth → the weight-read floor under every decode step (1.40 ms for 18.4 GB int8 on 16 v5e)

KV per token = 2·L·K·H·bytes → × context → per-sequence bytes → (HBM − weights) ÷ that = users that fit → 7 at 128k for the invented model, 56 with K = 1 → long context is a memory problem long before it is a compute problem

MoE multiplies MLP parameters by E for storage but only k per token for FLOPs → reuse per weight byte drops by E/k → B<sub>crit</sub> × E/k (240 → 1,920 tokens for E = 16, k = 2) while KV per token is unchanged

2D weight-stationary splits weights over both D and F → comms per chip fall as 1/√N → it beats 1D model sharding's constant 4BD/(3W) only past ≈ 72 chips → irrelevant at 4x4 or one 8-GPU node, important for very large slices
elevated: At Q2's full load a decode step reads 18.4 GB of weights plus 235 GB of KV → ≈ 19.3 ms → at 128k context, KV reads, not weights, set latency, and the Q3 floor is only a small part of it
reference: the invented model's hyperparameters (L = 64, D = 4,096, F = 16,384, N = 32, K = 8, H = 256, V = 32,128)
our Q4 and Q6 sharding answers (the book gives none)

compress.prompt: Without looking, write the four formulas you need most (parameter count, KV per token, users that fit, B<sub>crit</sub> for MoE) and next to each, the everyday question at an inference company it answers.
checklist: P = L·D·(3F + 2H(N+K)) + D·V → how big is the model, and what is the weight-read floor?
KV/token = 2·L·K·H·bytes → how much does each user's context cost?
(HBM − weights) ÷ (KV/token × context) → how many users of this context fit on this box?
B<sub>crit</sub> × E/k → how much batch does this MoE need before its FLOPs stop idling?

retrieve.q: Explain why Q2's answer (7 users at 128k) means the slice will be memory-bound no matter how the model is sharded.
answer: only 7 sequences fit, so the decode batch is 7 tokens per step
B<sub>crit</sub> for int8 × int8 on v5e is 240, far above 7
sharding changes which chip holds what, not how many sequences fit in total HBM

retrieve.q: Walk through Q5's total and active parameter counts for E = 16, k = 2: which term changes and by how much?
answer: only the MLP term 3·D·F scales: × E for total, × k for active
attention and embeddings unchanged, so KV per token stays 262 kB

retrieve.q: For Q4 decode you could model-shard 16 ways or keep 4-way model sharding and use the other axis differently. What does the card's arithmetic say decides it, and what does the extra sharding cost?
answer: decode is memory-bound, so reading fewer weight bytes per chip (1.15 GB at 16-way vs 4.60 GB at 4-way) cuts latency
the generation limit F/(B·β) = 16,384/(7·8) ≈ 293 ≫ 16, so comms don't bind on bandwidth
the cost: K = 8 < 16, so the KV must also be split on batch (two AllToAlls per layer), and small collectives pay ≈ 1 µs per hop

compare.q: Q2 asks how many users fit; Part 8 asks what a query costs. What does Part 8 add on top of Q2's arithmetic to get from fits to cost?
answer: a step time (KV + max(params, FLOPs)) at that batch
decode steps per query (512 in the book)
division by chips: QPS per chip, which is cost per query
and it varies slice size and precision instead of fixing them

compare.q: Q6 shards experts over one mesh axis and finds the weight-load time barely depends on batch. What causes that, and what does it mean for an MoE server at low traffic?
answer: each chip holds a fixed slice of experts and the step waits for the busiest chip
at modest batch most experts get some tokens, so that chip reads its whole slice anyway
so low traffic pays the full weight read per step; an MoE needs large batches (Q5's 1,920 tokens) to use its FLOPs

predict.q: Take the invented model but cut it to 48 layers (everything else the same). Commit first: how many 128k-token users fit on the v5e 4x4 in int8, and is the weight-load floor above or below 1 ms?
predict.answer: P = 48 · 4,096 · (3·16,384 + 2·256·40) + 4,096·32,128 = 13.82e9. KV per token = 2·48·8·256 = 196,608 B, so a 128k sequence is 25.2 GB. (256 − 13.8) / 25.2 = 9.6 → 9 users. The floor is 13.82e9 / 1.312e13 = 1.05 ms: just above 1 ms. Fewer layers shrink both the weights and the per-token KV by the same 3/4.

apply.task: Work Q1–Q3 again, on paper and without the card, for two variants of the invented model: (a) L = 48 layers; (b) L = 64 but K = 2 KV heads. For each give parameters, KV per token in int8, users that fit at 128k on a v5e 4x4 (256 GB), and the weight-load floor. Then check both with labs/worked-problems.py by editing its constants.
apply.done: (a) ≈ 13.82e9 params, 196,608 B/token, 9 users, ≈ 1.05 ms; (b) ≈ 17.57e9 params (only the attention term shrinks), 65,536 B/token, 28 users, ≈ 1.34 ms; and the lab agrees.
apply.hint: For (b), KV = 2·64·2·256 = 65,536 B, so a 128k sequence is 8.39 GB; (256 − 18.4)/8.39 ≈ 28.3. Recompute (b)'s parameters with N + K = 34 instead of 40 if you want the exact floor.
